note: Korean vowels are built from three symbols invented in 1443: · (the sun, now written as a short stroke), ㅡ (the flat earth) and ㅣ (a standing person). Every vowel below is a combination of those three. Teaching the system beats teaching twenty-one separate shapes.

building_blocks.role: the stroke added to a stem; written today as a short dash

placement_rule.vertical: Vowels built on ㅣ stand to the RIGHT of the consonant: ㅎ + ㅏ = 하
placement_rule.horizontal: Vowels built on ㅡ sit BELOW the consonant: ㅎ + ㅗ = 호
placement_rule.mixed: Vowels that use both wrap around the consonant: ㅎ + ㅘ = 화

y_rule: One stroke means a plain vowel. Two strokes means the same vowel with a y- glide in front: ㅏ→ㅑ (a→ya), ㅓ→ㅕ, ㅗ→ㅛ, ㅜ→ㅠ. Learn four pairs instead of eight letters.

vowels.name: 아
vowels.construction: A person with the sun to their right (east — where it rises).
vowels.english_hint: The a of 'father'. Open your mouth wide.
vowels.mouth: Jaw dropped, tongue low and flat, lips relaxed and unrounded.
vowels.common_error: Making it too short, like the a in 'cat'.

vowels.name: 야
vowels.construction: ㅏ with a second stroke — add a y.
vowels.mouth: Start at ㅣ, glide straight into ㅏ.
vowels.common_error: Dropping the y and saying ㅏ.

vowels.name: 어
vowels.construction: A person with the sun to their left (west — where it sets).
vowels.english_hint: Closest to the u of 'but' or the aw of 'saw' — but crucially your lips do NOT round.
vowels.mouth: Jaw half open, tongue back, lips completely relaxed and spread flat.
vowels.common_error: The single hardest vowel for English speakers. Almost everyone rounds their lips and produces ㅗ instead. Watch yourself in a mirror: if your lips move forward, it is wrong.

vowels.name: 여
vowels.construction: ㅓ with a second stroke — add a y.
vowels.english_hint: Like 'yuh'. The y of 'young' plus ㅓ.
vowels.mouth: Glide from ㅣ into ㅓ, lips unrounded throughout.
vowels.common_error: Rounding into 'yo' — that is ㅛ, a different letter.

vowels.name: 오
vowels.construction: The sun above the earth — sunrise.
vowels.english_hint: The o of 'go', but pure — no slide into a 'w' sound at the end.
vowels.mouth: Lips pushed forward into a tight circle, tongue back and high.
vowels.common_error: English 'o' is really a diphthong (oh-oo). Korean ㅗ holds one steady shape.

vowels.name: 요
vowels.construction: ㅗ with a second stroke — add a y.
vowels.mouth: Glide from ㅣ into ㅗ, lips rounding as you go.
vowels.common_error: None, usually — this is the polite ending -요, so you will say it constantly.

vowels.name: 우
vowels.construction: The sun below the earth — sunset.
vowels.mouth: Lips tightly rounded and pushed forward, tongue high and back.
vowels.common_error: Not rounding enough, which drifts toward ㅡ.

vowels.name: 유
vowels.construction: ㅜ with a second stroke — add a y.
vowels.mouth: Glide from ㅣ into ㅜ.
vowels.common_error: None.

vowels.name: 으
vowels.construction: The flat earth, on its own.
vowels.english_hint: English has no equivalent. Say 'ee' as in 'see', then — without moving your tongue — pull your lips back into a flat, wide smile. That is ㅡ.
vowels.mouth: Tongue high and back like ㅜ, but lips completely unrounded and spread.
vowels.common_error: Substituting 'oo' or the u of 'put'. Both round the lips; ㅡ never does. Second-hardest vowel after ㅓ.

vowels.name: 이
vowels.construction: A standing person, on their own.
vowels.mouth: Tongue high and forward, lips spread.
vowels.common_error: None.

vowels.name: 애
vowels.construction: ㅏ + ㅣ written together.
vowels.english_hint: The e of 'bed'. In modern Seoul speech it is nearly identical to ㅔ.
vowels.mouth: Jaw slightly lower than for ㅔ, in careful speech.
vowels.common_error: There is nothing to hear — the two have merged for most speakers under forty. Treat ㅐ vs ㅔ as a spelling problem, learned word by word.

vowels.name: 에
vowels.construction: ㅓ + ㅣ written together.
vowels.english_hint: The e of 'bed'. Nearly identical to ㅐ in modern speech.
vowels.mouth: Jaw slightly higher than for ㅐ, in careful speech.
vowels.common_error: Same as ㅐ — a spelling contrast, not a sound contrast.

vowels.name: 얘
vowels.construction: ㅑ + ㅣ.
vowels.english_hint: 'yeh'. Very rare — you will meet it in 얘기 and little else.
vowels.mouth: ㅣ gliding into ㅐ.
vowels.common_error: None; it is uncommon enough to learn per word.

vowels.name: 예
vowels.construction: ㅕ + ㅣ.
vowels.mouth: ㅣ gliding into ㅔ.
vowels.common_error: After a consonant it is usually simplified to ㅔ in speech: 시계 is said [시게].

vowels.name: 와
vowels.construction: ㅗ + ㅏ — and it sounds exactly like it looks.
vowels.mouth: Start rounded like ㅗ, open out into ㅏ.
vowels.common_error: None. The compound vowels are the friendliest part of Hangul: they sound like their parts added together.

vowels.name: 왜
vowels.construction: ㅗ + ㅐ.
vowels.mouth: ㅗ gliding into ㅐ.
vowels.common_error: ㅙ, ㅚ and ㅞ all sound the same for most speakers. Another spelling-only contrast.

vowels.name: 외
vowels.construction: ㅗ + ㅣ.
vowels.english_hint: 'weh'. Despite the romanisation 'oe', it is said like ㅞ by almost everyone.
vowels.mouth: ㅗ gliding into ㅔ.
vowels.common_error: Reading the romanisation literally as 'oh-eh'.

vowels.name: 워
vowels.construction: ㅜ + ㅓ.
vowels.mouth: ㅜ gliding into ㅓ — the lips unround as you go.
vowels.common_error: Keeping the lips rounded through the whole vowel, which turns it into ㅘ.

vowels.name: 웨
vowels.construction: ㅜ + ㅔ.
vowels.mouth: ㅜ gliding into ㅔ.
vowels.common_error: Rare in native words. Mostly appears in loanwords like 웨딩.

vowels.name: 위
vowels.construction: ㅜ + ㅣ.
vowels.mouth: ㅜ gliding into ㅣ.
vowels.common_error: None.

vowels.name: 의
vowels.construction: ㅡ + ㅣ.
vowels.english_hint: ㅡ sliding straight into ㅣ, said quickly. There is no English equivalent.
vowels.mouth: Start with flat spread lips at ㅡ and glide to ㅣ without rounding at any point.
vowels.common_error: ㅢ is the one vowel whose pronunciation depends on where it sits. At the start of a word it is a true ㅢ (의사). After a consonant it is simply [ㅣ] (희망 → [히망]). As the possessive particle it is usually [에] (저의 → [저에]). Three pronunciations, one spelling.
